impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that Teva's headache patents claiming methods of treating headache using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL invalidating Teva's headache patents under § 112, after a jury had found Eli Lilly willfully infringed and failed to prove invalidity. The court remanded for further proceedings, effectively reinstating the jury verdict finding infringement. This case has significant implications for the scope of pharmaceutical patent claims directed to genus antibody claims with functional limitations.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent holders' ability to obtain and enforce genus-level claims for biologic drugs, particularly antibody patents, by limiting the circumstances under which JMOL of invalidity can override a jury's findings on written description and enablement.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar drug developers face greater risk that broad antibody patent claims will survive validity challenges, potentially delaying market entry and increasing litigation costs.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly granted summary judgment of noninfringement of a multicore processor patent based on extraterritoriality and rejection of VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory, and whether the court properly struck certain damages expert theories.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed in part the summary judgment of noninfringement of VLSI's '836 patent relating to multicore processor task allocation, finding triable issues remained. The court affirmed in part and remanded for further proceedings. This high-profile case between a major patent assertion entity and Intel addresses the territorial reach of U.S. patent law in global semiconductor manufacturing.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting infringement against global technology manufacturers benefit from a broader view of when domestic patent infringement can be found despite overseas manufacturing activities.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies with global manufacturing operations face increased exposure to U.S. patent infringement claims, and the reversal signals that summary judgment on extraterritoriality grounds may be harder to obtain.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding Versata's trade secret damages expert and in overturning the jury's breach of contract damages award, and whether Ford was entitled to JMOL on trade secret misappropriation liability.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously excluded damages models. The court reversed the district court's override of the jury's breach of contract damages award, reinstating it, and affirmed Ford's liability for trade secret misappropriation under both the DTSA and Michigan law. The case involved Ford's development of competing configuration software after licensing Versata's products.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software licensors benefit from the court's affirmation that trade secret misappropriation liability can attach when a licensee develops competing software using knowledge gained during the license, and from the reinstatement of jury contract damages awards.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that license third-party software and later develop in-house alternatives face heightened trade secret misappropriation risk, and must carefully segregate licensed information from independent development efforts.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations had expired on Insulet's DTSA trade secret misappropriation claim before suit was filed, entitling EOFlow to judgment as a matter of law.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's denial of JMOL and held that Insulet's DTSA claim was time-barred, overturning a jury verdict finding misappropriation of four trade secrets related to insulin patch pump technology. The court determined that Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing suit, notwithstanding the jury's contrary finding on timeliness.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation benefit from strict enforcement of the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations, providing a powerful defense when the trade secret owner had early knowledge of potential misappropriation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners face significant risk of losing their claims if they delay filing suit, even when gathering evidence. Companies must act promptly once they discover or should have discovered potential misappropriation by former employees or competitors.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was a legally sufficient evidentiary basis for the jury's finding that each of the asserted trade secrets was a protectable trade secret under California law, and whether the related patent-invalidity and counterfeiting claims were properly decided.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret misappropriation claims, holding that the plaintiff failed to prove the asserted trade secrets were protectable because the claimed information was generally known. The court vacated the reasonable royalty, exemplary damages, and permanent injunction. However, it affirmed liability and damages on the counterfeiting claim for unauthorized use of the Penuma® mark, and reversed the denial of JMOL on patent invalidity.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in trade secret cases benefit from the court's rigorous application of the requirement that trade secret owners prove their information is not generally known, raising the evidentiary bar for plaintiffs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must ensure robust evidence that their claimed secrets are not generally known in the industry; otherwise, even a favorable jury verdict may be reversed on JMOL. Companies relying on trade secret protection must carefully document the novelty of their information.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the use of a single verdict question covering infringement for all asserted patents, a flawed jury instruction on § 101 validity, and the district court's § 101 rulings on the asserted patents required vacatur of the $11.5 million damages judgment.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the infringement and damages judgments ($11.5 million) and remanded for a new trial, finding that the verdict form's single infringement question covering all four asserted patents was prejudicial error because it made it impossible to determine which patent the jury found infringed. The court also vacated and remanded on § 101 eligibility for one patent while affirming eligibility for two others.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the requirement that verdict forms must allow juries to make separate infringement findings for each asserted patent, preventing improper bundling that obscures the basis of liability.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders risk having large damages awards vacated and retried if they use verdict forms that do not require separate findings per patent, increasing litigation costs and uncertainty.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of two patents directed to non-uniform constellation designs used in digital communications but affirmed eligibility for claims of two other patents. The court affirmed the denial of JMOL on infringement and damages, preserving the willful infringement finding and damages award for the eligible patents. The case addresses the § 101 boundary for communications technology patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in communications technology benefit from the affirmance of eligibility for specific implementation claims, and the preservation of damages and infringement findings provides certainty for licensing programs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies face continued uncertainty about § 101 eligibility for communications patents, as the court drew fine distinctions between claims within the same patent family, with some found eligible and others not.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the on-sale bar of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) applies based on sales of a prior art device, and whether Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative testimony outside personal knowledge is admissible at summary judgment.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that sales of a prior art device more than one year before the patent's priority date invalidated the asserted claims. The court also held that Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative testimony is admissible at summary judgment even when the witness lacks personal knowledge of the events, and that source code constitutes non-hearsay computer commands rather than statements.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the ruling that 30(b)(6) testimony is admissible regardless of personal knowledge and that source code is non-hearsay, making it easier to establish prior art invalidity defenses at summary judgment.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased vulnerability to on-sale bar challenges where corporate representatives can testify about historical sales without personal knowledge, lowering the evidentiary threshold for invalidity.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using relay devices on farming equipment are patent-ineligible abstract ideas under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the case was exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's patents for farming data collection and sharing systems were directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas under § 101, but vacated and remanded the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional. The ruling continues to limit patentability of data collection and processing claims in the agricultural technology space.
impacts.positiveImplications: Agricultural technology companies and other defendants facing patent assertions benefit from the continued application of § 101 to invalidate data-processing claims, and the remand on exceptionality may enable fee-shifting against weak patent assertions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies developing IoT and data analytics platforms for agriculture face significant barriers to patent protection, as claims involving data collection from sensors, processing, and sharing continue to be found abstract under Alice/Mayo.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly found that Apple's importation and sale of Apple Watch models with blood oxygen measurement features violated Section 337 of the Tariff Act by infringing Masimo's patents covering wearable blood oxygen measurement devices.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated Section 337 by importing Apple Watches that infringed Masimo's patents on wearable blood oxygenation measurement technology. The court upheld the limited exclusion order barring importation of infringing Apple Watch models, as well as the ITC's domestic industry determination, validity rulings, and infringement findings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders, particularly in the medical device and wearable technology space, benefit from the affirmance of ITC enforcement through exclusion orders against major technology companies, reinforcing the ITC as a powerful venue for patent enforcement.
impacts.negativeImplications: Major technology companies incorporating third-party patented technology into consumer products face substantial import-ban risk through ITC proceedings, potentially requiring product redesigns or licensing arrangements to maintain market access.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled declaratory judgment action when it had previously filed a declaratory judgment action and missed the deadline for seeking a stay.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the statutory deadline for seeking a mandatory stay of a parallel district court action by voluntarily dismissing and refiling the district court action after the deadline has passed. The ruling prevents gamesmanship in the coordination between ITC investigations and parallel district court patent litigation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders pursuing ITC investigations benefit from the ruling preventing respondents from manipulating filing deadlines to obtain mandatory stays, ensuring that parallel district court actions can proceed on schedule.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents who miss the 30-day deadline for requesting a mandatory stay cannot cure the deficiency by refiling the district court action, potentially forcing them to litigate in two forums simultaneously.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that has licensed exclusive commercialization rights but retained the right to sue for infringement retains constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that patent owners who retain the right to sue third parties for infringement maintain sufficient exclusionary rights for Article III standing, even after granting an exclusive license to commercialize the patents. The retained right to sue was not rendered illusory by the rights granted to the licensee.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners structuring license agreements can retain standing to enforce patents by carefully reserving litigation rights, providing flexibility to monetize patents through both licensing and enforcement.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a potentially dispositive standing defense where patent owners have retained litigation rights, even when substantial commercialization rights have been exclusively licensed to third parties.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB's obviousness determination should be vacated where a non-party to the underlying district court litigation filed IPR petitions on the same filing deadline as the sued party, and whether the Board properly denied termination of the proceedings.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness determination invalidating FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent and remanded for further proceedings. Qualcomm, which was not a party to the underlying infringement litigation, filed IPR petitions on the exact deadline applicable to the actual defendant, raising concerns about the use of third-party IPR petitions to circumvent the one-year time bar of § 315(b).
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from heightened scrutiny of IPR petitions filed by third parties that appear coordinated with actual defendants to circumvent the one-year time bar, protecting the integrity of the IPR system.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies seeking to challenge patent validity through IPR face greater risk that petitions filed near statutory deadlines by entities not involved in the underlying litigation will be scrutinized for improper coordination with the actual defendant.

impacts.caseName: mCom IP, LLC v. City National Bank of Florida
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court properly dismissed a patent infringement complaint on obviousness grounds at the pleading stage and whether the resulting § 285 exceptional-case fee award and § 1927 attorney sanctions were justified.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed dismissal of a patent infringement complaint for failure to state a claim, agreeing the surviving claims were invalid on the same obviousness grounds the PTAB applied to cancel other claims of the same patent. However, the court reversed the § 285 exceptional-case fee award and § 1927 attorney sanctions, finding insufficient grounds to declare the case exceptional or to conclude counsel acted in bad faith.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent litigants and their counsel benefit from the reversal of fee-shifting and sanctions, signaling that filing suit on surviving patent claims after an adverse IPR is not per se exceptional or sanctionable conduct.
impacts.negativeImplications: Defendants who successfully defeat patent claims at the pleading stage may find it harder to recover fees and costs, even when the patent has been substantially invalidated in IPR proceedings.

impacts.caseName: National Veterans Legal Services Program v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary charged excessive PACER fees beyond those authorized by statute, including the propriety of attorneys' fees and incentive awards to class representatives.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's approval of a $125 million settlement in a nationwide class action challenging the federal judiciary's use of PACER fees to fund projects unrelated to PACER operations. The court upheld the settlement, attorneys' fee awards, and incentive awards to the three nonprofit class representatives, rejecting an objector's challenges on jurisdiction, settlement fairness, and the permissibility of incentive awards.
impacts.positiveImplications: The resolution provides hundreds of thousands of PACER users with fee reimbursements, and the approval of incentive awards supports organizations willing to serve as class representatives in public-interest class actions.
